prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED as my first choice, but having read all eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks to the top of my preferred configuration. It is the only shortlisted candidate that every member ranked, five of us place it in the top three, and the two credited names are the same in every ballot. The physics is clean: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated at once, and Ye's group then showed what that buys, with record stability and accuracy and many-body effects under control. Clocks at the 10^-18 level are reproduced and compared across laboratories, they test relativity and constants, and they are the basis for the coming redefinition of the second. This is a discovery-and-measurement result with a robust independent confirmation record, which is the kind of maturity I look for before arguing for a prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Stefan Kroll and I would both be tempted to wave away: optical frequency metrology has been honoured twice recently (Hall and Haensch in 2005, Wineland and Haroche in 2012), so this can be read as a refinement of a recognised line rather than a new regime. A second concern is that Katori and Ye are a clean pair only if one accepts the lattice-clock concept as the discovery; Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups made real contributions that a two-name citation leaves out. Finally, Bernhard Mehlig's point that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened is fair, since recognition may be more natural once the community has settled on the new standard.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as measurement-limited progress that opens gravitational-redshift sensing, geodesy and searches for varying constants, and finds the Katori and Ye pair clean and defensible.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the pairing, and I now put it first. I would qualify one thing: the argument should rest on what the lattice clock made newly accessible (many-atom, quantum-limited interrogation and control of systematics at 10^-18) and not on the redefinition of the second, which is a standards decision and not a physics discovery. I also disagree mildly with Stefan's ranking of atom interferometry second. Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich have decisive early contributions, but Chu's closely related work was honoured in 1997 and Eva Lindroth herself notes the 1991 priority is shared among several groups, so that allocation is harder than the clock pair.

responses.point: Mehlig finds the clocks well understood and decisively confirmed but suggests a prize might be better timed after the redefinition of the SI second, and he ranks magic-angle graphene and topological insulators above it.
responses.response: I take the timing argument seriously but do not think we should wait. The discovery is complete and confirmed in several laboratories; the redefinition is a consequence, not a condition, and tying our decision to a metrological committee's schedule would make the prize hostage to something that does not change the science. On his preferred candidates, I share his admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald simplicity, but I rank twisted bilayer graphene lower because the pairing mechanism is still unsettled and the field is only about eight years old. Magic-angle graphene is where I would expect the committee to converge in a few years, and I would be comfortable with it as an alternative.

responses.point: Pearce, our chair, ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window, with Halzen and Karle as the core, and ranks the lattice clock second on control of systematics and independent reproduction.
responses.response: We agree on the clock and on the criteria of systematics control and independent reproduction. I do not feel qualified to judge IceCube beyond what is on the ballots, and I defer to Mark and Ulf on astroparticle physics. My one worry is the one Mark states himself: individual source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are at roughly 3 to 4 sigma and the origin of the diffuse flux is open, so maturity looks less settled than for the clocks. The lineage from AMANDA and Baikal also makes a three-name allocation harder than the two-name clock citation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks circuit QED seventh because a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 may look like engineering of a platform just recognised, and he ranks the clock eighth and defers to atomic physicists.
responses.response: I accept the substance of Olle's circuit-QED reservation and it is part of why I lowered my own first choice: the physics of strong coupling is distinct from macroscopic tunnelling, but the timing and balance concern is real, and I cannot judge it neutrally given my field. I would resist the idea that cQED is merely engineering, since it opened a new regime of single artificial-atom strong coupling and is a platform for fundamental quantum optics, but that is exactly why I list it as an alternative and not as my lead. On the clock, his deferral is reasonable; the colleagues in atomic physics (Lindroth, Kroll) ranked it first, and I give their judgment on relative standing considerable weight.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first as a precision atomic-physics result where theory and experiment agree and the result is robust, while noting that Lemonde, Gill, Hinkley and Ludlow are not credited and the comb side was honoured in 2005.
responses.response: I agree and think her note on the credit boundary is the right one to carry into later rounds. I would keep the citation about the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 10^-18, which protects against reading it as a prize for all optical clocks. I also share her view that the principal impact of squeezed light came through the detectors recognised in 2017, which is why I keep squeezing out of my preferred configuration even though I ranked it sixth.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads optical lattice clocks as a distinct achievement or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes on optical frequency metrology.
Whether Katori and Ye adequately represent the lattice-clock contributions of Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow and others, and how much weight strontium versus ytterbium work should carry.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, and whether a circuits-centred prize (B021) is balanced against the 2025 award.
How much condensed-matter weight to give B015 and B053, which are outside my primary field and where I defer partly to colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits, so B021 (circuit QED) falls squarely in my own field and I should recuse myself from deciding it, as should be noted for the record; I also have professional ties to Chalmers colleagues in this area. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B057, B015 or the other shortlisted candidates.
